A study compared recovery outcomes in children with persistent diarrhea who were fed a milk-based diet containing 6 g/kg/day of lactose versus the same diet pre-treated with β-galactosidase. The results indicated differences in recovery rates. 2. In Australia, a study among hospitalized Aboriginal children evaluated three formulas with varying osmolality and protein hydrolysis. Two lactose-free formulas (De-Lact and O-Lac) reduced diarrhea duration compared to a partially hydrolyzed formula (Alfare). De-Lact, a low-osmolality lactose-free formula, also improved the lactulose-to-rhamnose (L/R) ratio compared to Alfare. 3. A Canadian study on children hospitalized with severe gastroenteritis found that those on a lactose-based diet experienced longer diarrhea duration, higher relapse rates, and greater stool output compared to those on a glucose-based diet. 4. Other studies have not consistently replicated these findings, likely due to variations in study design, sample characteristics, and the type of diarrhea (acute vs. persistent). 5. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Peru compared four dietary regimens for children aged 3–24 months with diarrhea. Lactose content in milk did not significantly affect clinical outcomes. However, combining wheat-based diets with milk products resulted in lower treatment failure rates and better diarrhea outcomes (shorter duration and reduced fecal output) compared to milk products alone. 6. In India, an RCT compared a milk-free diet (rice, lentil, sugar, and coconut oil) to a commercial cow’s milk formula in children with acute diarrhea. Another older study in Guatemala showed reduced stool frequency in malnourished children given β-galactosidase-treated milk compared to untreated cow’s milk, though other outcomes like recovery and growth were not significantly different. 7. Regarding cow’s milk osmolality, an equivalence trial in Guatemalan and Brazilian infants aged 2 weeks to 6 months with diarrhea found no differences in treatment failure, stool output, or diarrhea duration between full-strength and diluted milk. 8. Glutamine supplementation has shown benefits in improving intestinal absorption and weight gain in adults with HIV. In animal models of cholera and Cryptosporidium infection, glutamine enhanced sodium and water absorption. However, an RCT in Brazil among malnourished infants found no improvement in diarrhea outcomes with glutamine added to oral rehydration solution (ORS). 9. Probiotics, such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactobacillus bulgaricus, and Streptococcus thermophilus, have been shown to reduce diarrhea frequency and duration in well-nourished children. Evidence in malnourished children is mixed. An RCT in Malawi using Synbiotic 2000 Forte added to ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) showed no significant improvements in nutritional cure or diarrhea morbidity, except for severe diarrhea among inpatients. 10. In India, adding Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG to ORS significantly reduced diarrhea frequency, duration, intravenous therapy requirements, and hospital stay in children with acute diarrhea. However, no subgroup analysis was conducted for malnourished children. 11. Zinc supplementation is recommended by WHO and UNICEF as adjunct therapy with ORS for diarrhea treatment. For children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), daily zinc supplementation (2 mg/kg/day) for at least two weeks is advised. Evidence on zinc’s efficacy in SAM-related diarrhea is limited. Two RCTs in India showed that zinc reduced diarrhea incidence, prolonged episodes, and recurrence, particularly when initiated within three days of onset. 12. A study in Bangladesh found zinc supplementation reduced diarrhea duration in malnourished children, with greater benefits observed in stunted children. Another trial in Bangladesh focusing on persistent diarrhea showed zinc reduced illness duration in underweight children. An RCT in Turkey demonstrated that zinc reduced prolonged diarrhea prevalence and stool frequency by day 4 in malnourished children. 13. In Pakistan, an RCT among hospitalized malnourished children found no significant differences in diarrhea morbidity or anthropometry with zinc supplementation. 14. Direct evidence for specific interventions in children with SAM receiving outpatient therapeutic feeding and diarrhea is lacking. Clinicians must rely on indirect evidence and pathophysiological understanding of SAM. Liberal use of electrolyte-containing fluids in SAM carries risks due to fragile homeostasis and should only be administered when dehydration is objectively confirmed. 15. Most diarrhea in malnourished children is not associated with dehydration. Clinical history is crucial for assessing dehydration in SAM. Rehydration should be achieved orally using low-osmolality solutions like ReSoMal, with careful monitoring of vital signs and weight. 16. If dehydration is absent, diarrhea does not require changes in SAM management. Caregivers should continue offering RUTF and allow children to drink water ad libitum. 17. Studies on modified feeding strategies for SAM and diarrhea are limited. Trials in Malawi showed higher recovery rates and weight gain with RUTF compared to standard treatment, though diarrhea prevalence was not consistently reduced. 18. Evidence on probiotics and prebiotics in malnourished children is heterogeneous. While probiotics reduced diarrhea in well-nourished children, findings in malnourished populations are mixed. Probiotics added to ORS in India reduced diarrhea frequency and duration, but no consistent benefits were observed in other settings. 19. Antiparasitics like nitazoxanide have shown efficacy in treating Cryptosporidium infections in HIV-uninfected children, improving diarrhea resolution and pathogen eradication. 20. There is limited evidence supporting lactose hydrolysis in milk-based feeding regimens for persistent diarrhea or glutamine supplementation in malnourished children with diarrhea. Further studies are needed to assess these interventions in children with SAM and diarrhea.
